column4: This is the section's full creditor-debtor scene: ذُو عُسْرَةٍ is granted time إِلَىٰ مَيْسَرَةٍ, while relinquishing the claim as charity is named the better course.

Repentance from usury leaves the creditor only رُءُوسُ أَمْوَالِكُمْ, the principal itself; this makes the section's measurable lowering of a claim precise and bars both creditor and debtor from injustice.
The creditor is ordered to abandon مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ ٱلرِّبَوٰٓا۟, the outstanding usurious balance; 2:279 defines the remaining lawful principal and 2:280 then addresses an insolvent debtor.

A debt due at a fixed term is to be written and witnessed, and فَتُذَكِّرَ إِحْدَىٰهُمَا ٱلْأُخْرَىٰ makes remembering part of preserving the claim; this is the Qur'anic realization of the section's “dhikr” as debt deed.
Support is scaled to actual means—ذُو سَعَةٍ from his abundance and the person whose provision is restricted from what God gave him—before the exact promise that God will make ease after hardship.
The same divine addressee was found عَآئِلًا and enriched; it supplies the section's concrete movement from an empty hand to financial sufficiency.

A voluntary outlay is cast as a “good loan” to God that He multiplies, while وَٱللَّهُ يَقْبِضُ وَيَبْصُطُ names constriction and expansion together; the human creditor's reduced claim thus enters a larger divine account.
Alms are assigned explicitly to ٱلْغَٰرِمِينَ, people burdened by debt, turning charitable giving into direct relief of the section's debtor.

Joseph's brothers arrive with بِبِضَٰعَةٍ مُّزْجَىٰةٍ, deficient purchasing capital, and ask him both to give full measure and to treat them charitably; scarcity, trade, and voluntary remission meet in one scene.
When asked what to spend, the answer is ٱلْعَفْوَ, the surplus; this directly matches the section's dictionary measure of charity as what remains beyond one's dependants.
The divorce gift is assessed عَلَى ٱلْمُوسِعِ قَدَرُهُۥ وَعَلَى ٱلْمُقْتِرِ قَدَرُهُۥ, making abundance and constraint measurable bases for a financial obligation just as in 65:7.
The payer must house and maintain the women according to his means and must not pressure them to constrict them; 65:7 then specifies spending by abundance or restricted provision.
The father owes food and clothing on a fair basis, yet no soul is charged beyond its capacity; this supplies the dependants whose due is met before the section's surplus becomes voluntary charity.
People of bounty and abundance are told to continue giving to vulnerable kin and to pardon and overlook; material width and relinquishing a due are joined as the creditor's generous stance.
God effaces usurious gain and causes charities to grow, reversing an ordinary creditor's account: increase through debt is loss, while what is given away increases.
Collateral, entrusted repayment, and the duty not to conceal testimony continue the written-debt scene of 2:282 and show how a claim is preserved when a scribe is unavailable.
وَيَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ uses the same “put down from them” construction for removing a binding burden; it confirms the section's hearing of وَضَعْنَا عَنكَ as concrete release from liability.

The question whether the messenger demands payment so that people are مِن مَّغْرَمٍ مُّثْقَلُونَ depicts an assessed debt as an actual crushing weight, precisely joining the section's debt and burden images.
This repeated question likewise pictures an demanded fee as a debt under which the addressees are weighed down, giving bodily force to the liability lifted in the section.
The branch leading to ease begins with the person who gives and is mindful; 92:7 names the resulting “ease,” so generosity occupies the creditor's side of the section's choice.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises facilitation toward ease after the giving of 92:5, joining the y-s-r root to openhanded conduct.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ turns the section's paired roots into a moral reversal: withholding and imagined self-sufficiency lead toward hardship rather than away from it.
The one who gives his wealth to purify himself embodies the freely given charity that, in the section, can take the form of cancelling a debtor's claim.
حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا is literally an easy reckoning, bringing the section's y-s-r promise and its account-book hearing into the same phrase.
وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ is another divine promise of ease to the prophetic addressee, supporting the personal promise heard through the section's financial sense of yusr.

God wills ٱلْيُسْرَ and not ٱلْعُسْرَ in the fasting law; the nonfinancial legal use clarifies that the financial narrowness in the section is one concrete instance of a broader divine preference for relief.
Within the same divorce legislation, God makes ease in the affair of one who is mindful; 65:7 then gives that ease a specifically financial form after hardship.
Satan threatens poverty when one spends, whereas God promises forgiveness and bounty; it exposes the fear of an emptied hand that can stop a creditor from remitting a claim.
God expands or restricts provision, and whatever the addressee spends He replaces; this directly answers the section's tension between giving from one's means and fear of diminished capital.

Immediately after the rule against a clenched or wholly outspread hand, God is said to expand and restrict provision; the giver's limit is placed inside the divine movement between width and scarcity.
A “good loan” to God is paired with almsgiving and answered by the erasure of wrongs, recasting voluntary expenditure as a debt whose divine creditor remits rather than presses.
The good loan to God is multiplied and rewarded generously, reversing the loss feared when capital leaves the giver's hand.
Men and women who give charity are themselves described as lending God a good loan, so charitable release and a creditor-debtor account are explicitly fused.
If people lend God a good loan, He multiplies it and forgives them; increase and remission occupy the same divine account that the section evokes.
The good loan is sent ahead and found with God better and greater in reward, making apparently reduced present wealth a credit preserved in another ledger.
حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ ٱلْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا joins the section's verb “put down” to its burden noun: even war ends by laying down its loads.

وَوُضِعَ ٱلْكِتَٰبُ places the comprehensive record before its debtors, while nothing small or great is omitted; it is a direct Qur'anic counterpart to the section's account book made concrete by وضع.
Those who deny the meeting carry أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ, making liability a load on the back; the section's cancelled debt gives equally concrete measure to that load's removal.

An enslaved person who seeks a written emancipation contract is to receive one when good is known, and the holder must give from God's wealth; a binding written liability is answered by material help from the party with power.

The surrounding passage distinguishes lawful trade from usury; that boundary prevents the section's commercial vocabulary of capital and loss from turning creditor profit into a justification for pressing the distressed debtor.
What is given as usury to grow through people's wealth does not grow with God, whereas zakat is multiplied; apparent account-book gain and charitable decrease exchange outcomes.
Usury that is multiplied again and again is the precise opposite of lowering a claim from an insolvent debtor's account.
The counterfigure withholds and deems himself self-sufficient; 92:10 sends him toward hardship, reversing the creditor whose abundance becomes relief for another.
His wealth does not avail him when he falls, setting a boundary on the imagined security of the retained capital described in 92:8.
The hand may be neither chained to the neck nor extended completely; it gives the section's “back of wealth” rule a Qur'anic boundary between miserliness and spending that leaves the giver destitute.

Those praised spend in prosperity and adversity and pardon people; this extends the section's surplus-based measure by showing that generosity and relinquishment can remain virtues even in one's own straitness.
The Helpers prefer others despite privation in themselves, a specific exceptional generosity beyond the section's ordinary measure of giving from surplus.
The mockers deride donors who can find only their utmost effort; the ayah protects sincere giving from scarce means and marks the limit of judging charity only by surplus size.
Hoarded gold and silver are condemned precisely because they are not spent in God's path; retained surplus becomes culpable rather than safe capital.
The hoarded wealth is heated and brands foreheads, sides, and ظُهُور; wealth withheld from giving becomes a load and mark on the very back invoked by the section.
The person given his book from behind his back reverses the joyful easy account of 84:7-9; the section's back and ledger images meet on the adverse side of reckoning.

The exchange of guidance for error is said to be a trade that did not profit; it supplies the Qur'anic reversal of the section's dictionary sense “to be put down in one's trade,” a loss larger than capital.
Generous recitation, prayer, and spending are called a trade that will never perish, the positive reversal of the section's commercial loss.
God pays such traders their rewards in full and adds from His bounty, answering diminished worldly capital with an undiminished divine settlement.
A person reads expanded provision as proof that God has honored him; 89:16 exposes the matching interpretation of restricted provision, and the passage rejects wealth as that simple moral account.
When provision is measured tightly, the person says God has humiliated him; the section instead hears hardship beside promised ease, not as a final verdict on worth.
Unlimited expansion of provision would make people transgress, so God sends it in due measure; this gives a boundary to the section's equation of width with desirable relief.
At death the person asks for a brief delay so that he can give charity; this reverses 2:280, where the living creditor can grant a debtor time and turn the claim itself into charity.
God will not delay a soul once its term arrives, marking the absolute boundary against which a human creditor's merciful extension in 2:280 is meaningful.

Between debt relief and debt documentation comes the day when every soul is paid in full for what it earned; the placement turns the human account into a reminder of the final settlement without erasing 2:280's mercy.
Between the destruction of usury and the order to abandon its remainder, believers who give zakat are promised their reward, keeping charitable circulation beside the creditor's relinquished gain.
Inheritance shares are distributed only after any bequest and debt; an outstanding debt is thus a quantifiable charge deducted from an estate before wealth reaches heirs.
The repeated priority of bequest and debt in the spouse and sibling shares shows the creditor's written claim surviving the debtor's death, a legal edge to the section's remissible burden.
The taking of usury and consuming people's wealth wrongfully are paired, placing creditor profit beyond principal on the unjust side of the section's scene.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury; it supplies the humane manner required when a creditor chooses relief rather than humiliating a distressed debtor.
The giver must not cancel charity's value by reminders and hurt, a concrete warning against turning voluntary relief into another form of pressure on its recipient.
The poor may appear self-sufficient because restraint keeps them from importunate asking; a creditor therefore cannot infer ease from silence when judging whether a debtor is truly in hardship.
Kin, the needy, and the traveler are to receive their due before the warning against waste; it helps specify the prior claims on wealth behind the section's reference to dependants.
Righteous spending is neither extravagant nor stingy but proportionate between them, another Qur'anic measure for the section's charity from available means.
Divorced women have a fair provision as a due, continuing the same means-sensitive family obligations that 2:236 and 65:7 quantify.
The wealthy guardian must abstain from an orphan's property, the poor guardian may take reasonably, and witnesses attend its return; means, entrusted capital, and an accountable transfer meet here.
After the addressee is reminded that God enriched him, he is forbidden to subdue the orphan; received abundance is thus made a reason not to exercise power harshly over someone vulnerable.
The same enriched addressee must not repel the petitioner, closely matching the creditor stance of not pressing or humiliating the person whose hand is empty.
The addressee is to recount his Lord's favor after being enriched; his fuller hand remains a remembered gift rather than self-owned proof of superiority over the debtor.
God expands provision for whom He wills and measures it tightly, while worldly abundance is only a brief enjoyment; this relativizes both parties' present positions in the debt scene.

After Qarun and his house are swallowed, the onlookers recognize that God expands and restricts provision; it stages an abrupt movement from conspicuous wealth to loss behind the section's lexical definition of entering hardship.
God's expansion and restriction of provision for His servants gives the section's financial width and narrowness a repeated providential frame.
The alternation of expanded and restricted provision is called a sign, reinforcing that the debtor's present scarcity is a condition that can change rather than a fixed identity.
God alone expands and restricts provision, challenging the wealthy person's assumption that possession itself secures status in the section's creditor-debtor relation.
The repeated sign of provision expanded or measured tightly keeps both creditor abundance and debtor hardship contingent on God.
The One who owns the keys of heaven and earth expands and restricts provision; the parties' unequal hands are located within a larger ownership than their private account.
وَأَنَّهُۥ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ attributes enrichment and sufficiency to God, echoing the agent of the addressee's change from poverty in 93:8.
The poor who marry are promised enrichment from God's bounty, another concrete promise that present lack of means need not remain permanent.
The beggar and deprived person possess a “right” in the generous person's wealth; beside the creditor's documented right, the section thus reveals a counterclaim made by need itself.
The worshippers recognize a known right in their wealth, converting surplus from mere possession into an accounted obligation.
That known right belongs to the petitioner and deprived, completing the reversal in which the person with means is also a debtor to the person in need.
Some Bedouins treat what they spend as مَغْرَمًا, an imposed financial loss or liability; this is the resentful opposite of freely turning a claim into charity.
The ruined garden owner turns his palms over what he spent on it, giving the section's “loss in trade” a visible scene of capital irretrievably gone.
The record is set down for judgment and the matter is settled justly; like 18:49, وَوُضِعَ ٱلْكِتَٰبُ links the section's named root with an actual ledger.
Receiving one's book in the right hand supplies the document immediately before the “easy account” of 84:8; the cited ayah contributes the favorable ledger and hand.
Joyful return to one's people is the outcome of the easy account in 84:8, completing the release rather than the calculation itself.
The recipient of the book behind his back calls for destruction, supplying the debtor-like dread on the adverse side of the account begun in 84:10.
Entering the blaze completes the consequence of that adverse ledger; this row contributes the enforced settlement, while 84:10 contributes the book behind the back.
